As Nigeria prepare to take on Japan in the final of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco, individual brilliance, tactical discipline and the ability to produce match-winning performances could determine which nation gets its hands on the trophy.
The Flamingos have earned their place in the final through a remarkable run of resilience, bouncing back from their opening-day defeat to Poland to record five consecutive victories. Japan, meanwhile, have demonstrated their quality throughout the competition, combining technical precision with attacking efficiency to reach another final.
Both teams possess players capable of changing the course of the contest. For Nigeria, the attacking threat has come from different sources at different stages, while Japan have relied on a well-organised collective built around some outstanding individual performers.
However, one of the most fascinating aspects of Nigeria’s campaign has been the emergence of a different match-winner in almost every game.
One of Nigeria’s biggest strengths heading into the final has been the depth of match-winning quality within the squad. Rather than depending on one individual to carry the team, different players have stepped forward whenever the occasion demanded.
That variety has been reflected in the Player of the Match awards, with five different Nigerian players receiving the honour across six matches at this edition of the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.
Oluwakemi Adegbuyi was recognised following Nigeria’s 2-0 victory over Puerto Rico, before Kanyinsola Yusuf took the spotlight in the 3-1 win against Korea DPR.

Oluebube Umejiaku earned the award after the 2-1 victory over Mexico, while Favour Nkwocha was rewarded for her contribution against Venezuela in the quarter-finals. Awawu Bashiru then produced a memorable performance against Brazil, scoring twice in the 3-1 semi-final triumph to become the latest Flamingos player to claim the individual accolade.
The achievement highlights Nigeria’s ability to find a new leader depending on the demands of a particular match, the opposition and the players selected in the starting eleven. It is an advantage that could prove decisive against Japan, especially if the final becomes a contest of endurance, tactical adjustments and individual moments of inspiration.
However, PREMIUM TIMES take a look at Six of the very best from both sides who could decide the Final on their day.
With three goals already to her name, Umejiaku has established herself as one of Nigeria’s most influential attacking players in Morocco.
Beyond her goalscoring contribution, the forward has demonstrated an ability to create problems for opposing defences through her movement, intelligent positioning and willingness to attack spaces behind the backline.
She also provided an assist in the victory over Puerto Rico and played a crucial role in Nigeria’s quarter-final success against Venezuela, winning the penalty that ultimately settled the contest.
Against Japan, her ability to stretch the defence and exploit spaces between the defenders could offer Nigeria an important attacking outlet. If she can reproduce the sharpness and movement that have characterised her performances throughout the tournament, Umejiaku could become a major problem for the Japanese backline.
Kurita has emerged as one of Japan’s most dangerous attacking players, scoring four goals in the tournament and establishing herself as a major threat in the final third.
Her contribution includes the winning goal against Ghana in the quarter-finals, further demonstrating her ability to deliver when the pressure is highest.
The forward’s movement, composure in front of goal and finishing ability make her a player Nigeria cannot afford to give too much freedom. Japan’s attacking approach often relies on quick combinations and intelligent movement, and Kurita’s ability to find spaces in the penalty area could punish any lapse in concentration.
Nigeria’s defenders will need to remain alert to her positioning and ensure she is not allowed to receive the ball comfortably in dangerous areas.
Adegbuyi has been another important figure in Nigeria’s attacking setup, contributing two goals while also playing a part in the team’s combination play in the final third.
The forward’s influence is not limited to finding the back of the net. Her involvement in the build-up to Queen Joseph’s goal against Brazil in the semi-final offered another indication of her ability to create opportunities for teammates and contribute to Nigeria’s attacking patterns.
Her understanding of space, link-up play and willingness to get involved in dangerous areas could be particularly valuable against a Japanese side that is comfortable keeping possession and organising its defensive structure.
With the final likely to demand patience and precision in front of goal, Adegbuyi’s ability to contribute both as a scorer and creator could be important to Nigeria’s chances.
Already identified as one of Japan’s key midfield figures before the tournament began, Matsushita has lived up to expectations as an important part of the team’s structure.
The defensive midfielder brings composure and intelligence to Japan’s play, combining her ability to retain possession with an impressive understanding of when to disrupt opposition attacks.
Her role could become particularly significant in the final, where the battle for control of midfield may determine how effectively both teams impose their preferred style.
Nigeria will need to find ways to limit her influence, prevent her from dictating the tempo and disrupt the passing combinations that allow Japan to build attacks from the middle of the pitch.
If Matsushita is given too much time and space, she could help Japan establish the control that has made them such a difficult opponent throughout the competition.
The Flamingos on field captain in the absence of Chidi Harmony on the field of play, will have a significant responsibility in ensuring Nigeria remain organised against one of the competition’s most dangerous attacking teams.
Japan have scored 14 goals on their way to the final, underlining the threat they pose when given time and space to build attacks. Oduntan’s leadership, defensive awareness and ability to maintain discipline will therefore be crucial as Nigeria attempt to contain the Japanese forward line.
Beyond her individual defensive responsibilities, the captain will also need to help keep her teammates organised, particularly during difficult periods when Japan are likely to enjoy spells of possession.
For Nigeria to stand a strong chance of lifting the trophy, Oduntan’s influence at the back could be just as important as the contributions of the attackers at the other end.
Japan’s goalkeeper, Kadowaki, has already demonstrated her ability to influence major moments, producing a decisive penalty save during the semi-final victory over Korea DPR.
Her intervention helped Japan survive a tense contest that eventually went to a penalty shootout, and the experience is likely to have strengthened her confidence ahead of the final.
For Nigeria, the challenge will be to test her with purposeful attempts rather than simply accumulating shots. The Flamingos have shown their capacity to create opportunities, particularly in the semi-final against Brazil, when they registered 35 attempts compared to Brazil’s seven.
They will need to bring that attacking ambition into the final while ensuring their efforts are accurate, well-timed and difficult for Kadowaki to deal with.
The meeting between Nigeria and Japan promises to be a fascinating contest between two teams with different strengths but the same ambition of becoming world champions.
Japan have been impressive with their technical quality, defensive organisation and attacking efficiency. Nigeria, on the other hand, have shown remarkable resilience and an ability to produce different match-winners throughout their journey to the final.
The Flamingos’ five different Player of the Match winners underline a collective strength that could become a major advantage. Japan may have their own standout performers, but Nigeria have repeatedly shown that the responsibility can be shared across the squad.
With Umejiaku and Adegbuyi offering attacking threats, Oduntan leading the defensive effort, and five different players already stepping up for individual recognition, Nigeria have several avenues through which they can hurt their opponents.
However, they must also be prepared for the threat posed by Kurita, the midfield influence of Matsushita and the confidence of Kadowaki between the posts.
For the Flamingos, this is more than another match. It is an opportunity to turn a historic campaign into a historic triumph and become the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.
The stage is set. Now, Nigeria must find the performance to finish the job.
